frameworks.name: Two-Question Decision Razor
frameworks.definition: A decision-making framework that asks 'What do I want to have happen?' and 'What increases the odds of that happening?' to override initial reactive impulses.

claims.text: Most people live reactively from impulse to impulse without examining whether their initial reaction aligns with their desired outcome. Alex Hormozi describes this pattern as living 'from gut reaction to gut reaction to gut reaction and then counter reaction,' likening it to being 'seaweed in the ocean' with no direction.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: A countermeasure impulse—the desire to punish, control, or retaliate against someone who has wronged you—is the opposite of what increases the odds of your desired outcome, because retaliation amplifies the other person's negative behavior toward you rather than resolving it.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: someone has taken an action you dislike
claims.mechanism: Retaliation triggers reciprocal escalation; non-engagement removes the stimulus for further action.

claims.text: When someone criticizes you online, responding to defend yourself or counter-attack increases the likelihood they will hate you more and escalate their campaign against you, rather than the outcome you want (which is for them to move on and forget about you).
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: someone says something bad about you publicly
claims.mechanism: Interaction reinforces the initial harm and prolongs the person's focus on you, when non-engagement allows natural decay of interest.

claims.text: When an employee is performing poorly, the immediate impulse to yell at or punish them decreases the likelihood they will improve, because it increases their anxiety and degradation, whereas positive recognition of one small thing they did well creates a feedback loop that encourages more of that behavior.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Punishment triggers anxiety and reduces cognitive capacity; positive reinforcement creates emotional safety and behavior repetition.

claims.text: Applying the two-question decision frame—'What do I want to have happen?' and 'What increases the odds of that happening?'—almost always reveals that the action that increases your odds is not your initial gut reaction.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Inaction—doing nothing at all—is often the highest-probability action for achieving your desired outcome in interpersonal conflict, because it avoids triggering escalation and allows the situation to resolve naturally.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: someone has done something you dislike
claims.mechanism: Inaction removes the stimulus for reciprocal response; the other party has no reason to continue escalating if you do not engage.
bounded_by: Does not apply to situations requiring immediate operational response (e.g., critical safety, legal, or business-continuity issues)
Does not apply when a decision itself must be made and delegated

claims.text: The tension in choosing inaction is that while it is physically efficient (no energy spent), it is emotionally painful (you want to react) because your initial impulse feels urgent and justified.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

examples.text: A person says something bad about you online. Your immediate impulse is to respond publicly and punish them back. But when you ask yourself 'What do I want to have happen?' the answer is 'I want this person to move on with their lives and forget that I exist.' Then you ask 'What increases the odds of that?' and the answer is clearly not responding, because responding reinforces that you noticed and cared, which extends the conflict.

An employee is doing a bad job. Your immediate reaction is to yell at them. But if you ask 'What do I want to have happen?' it's 'I want them to do a good job.' If you then ask 'Does yelling increase the odds of that?' the honest answer is no—it makes them more anxious and they perform worse. So instead you find one thing they did well and publicly recognize them for it, which creates a positive loop they can see and want to repeat.

practices.text: When facing an interpersonal conflict or someone doing something you don't want them to do, stop and ask yourself two questions: (1) What do I want to have happen? and (2) What increases the odds of that happening?
In business and interpersonal relationships, prioritize maintaining focus on your core work, your marriage, and doing good work—ignore noise and attempts to provoke you.
